185982:
TO:

Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy Members of the Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs

FROM: Christopher Anderson, Advisor and Instructor, Southern Maine Community College RE: Testimony in support of LD 680, An Act to Support Higher Education in Maine by
Providing Funds to Maine's Community Colleges DATE: March 17, 2025

Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on
Education and Cultural Affairs, I am Chris Anderson, I live in Falmouth, ME, and I am an Advisor and part of the faculty of English at Southern Maine Community College. I am here
today in support of LD 680, An Act to Support Higher Education in Maine by Providing Funds
to Maine`s Community Colleges.

Over the past four years, 17,151 Free-College eligible students have enrolled in MCCS. The
direct from high school class increased by 1,000 students in 2 years and is expected to stabilize at
28% of a graduating class, equal to 3,500 students. These numbers are in sync with Strategy A in
Maine's 2020-2029 Economic Development Strategy, which is to grow local talent by increasing
access to activities in MCCS. But, who will support them?
Expanding access to education in MCCS in order to grow and retain local talent without also
increasing the staff to support those students is ethically irresponsible. It wastes taxpayer dollars
by enrolling students who will drop out. Study after study demonstrate a correlation between creating a human connection at college and completing a credential. As more courses move
online and dependency on adjunct teaching increases, support staff are vital to student success. Successful students turn into financially responsible citizens that support their local community. The success of these students will shape our future lives.
My advising case load is over 300 students, plus 80 from teaching. I'm not special. All carry these loads and almost 50% of our staff advisors also teach. We had ten staff advisors a year ago,
soon we will have seven. Shrinking by a third means 125 more students. When will I see them?

Though many student concerns are acute, average wait time is three weeks. I suppose now it will
be four. That's a quarter of our l6-week semester or half of our eight-week semester.
I love education. I didn't enter it for the money. I was quite aware that staff are compensated at
levels below what most of the students we teach and advise will earn. I chose to work at a
Community College. MCCS provides practical skills to anyone, at any level, to make their life
better. In this sense, I don't just love it, I believe in it. I believe in its ability to transform people's lives. And, this is not a power I have faith in. It's a power I see in full every week. People taking
steps to make their lives better, the lives of their family better, the lives of their neighbors better in the face of severe adversity. Few institutions can really claim that. The formula for increasing the results of this are simple -- we need you to believe in the power of education as well. To
believe in MCCS as a tool to ensure that the communities throughout Maine have a future.
This money is a conservative investment. There is no risk. There are well-documented links between student success and pathway advising. Without money to hire and retain staff to meet the needs of increasing student enrollment, we can't do pathway advising. Your vote will have
deep reverberations, impacting not only staff and students, but the future communities where our students end up living and working. Thank you for your time.

DATE: March 17, 2025
Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Education
and Cultural Affairs, I am David Daigler, President of the Maine Community College System.
I would like to start by thanking President Daughtry for her unwavering support of the Maine Community College System, our students and staff, and, in fact, all of higher education in Maine.
I am here to today to support LD680, aptly named An Act to Support Higher Education in Maine by
Providing Funds to Maine's Community Colleges.
The funds in this bill will directly assist the students at Maine's community colleges and through that, all of Maine. Our colleges are widening the pipeline for more skilled graduates entering the workforce and
increasing transfers to our four-year college partners.
At the State of MCCS last Tuesday, you heard me tell stories of students who overcame their anxieties,
worked hard and are either on their way to graduating or who have already graduated and are beginning
successful careers.
Their success relied on the dedication of our staff --- working with very limited resources -- who
assisted those same students with counseling, state and federal benefit paperwork, academic tutoring, housing, childcare, food, clothing and sometimes just a cup of coffee and a pep talk.
During the budget hearings, you heard directly from students. I think about the power of those stories
every day. I am grateful that they took the time to share their stories with you and I realize that the fact that they took the time to come to Augusta is indicative of how important our work is to them.
I often hear directly from staff and faculty -- full-time and adjuncts -- about the stress they feel every
day. It is not in their constitution to ignore a student in need, but they need more resources to serve our
students. They do what they can with what they have, but they are being worked to -- and often beyond
--- their limit.

That is why I stand before you today.
There is no denying that many of today's pre-K-12 students simply didn't get the same education as their peers who came to college before the pandemic.
It is not their fault. It is not the secondary school's fault.
Face-to-face hours in the classroom were disrupted, large numbers of teachers were out and substitutes filled in sometimes for extended periods, students were struggling with personal and family issues and isolation that distracted them from their education and delayed some of their coping and interpersonal
skills. As those students enter our colleges, as they will continue to for the next decade, we recognize
that they need additional academic support -- more tutoring, more time with professors, help with writing papers or using the library. They need more emotional support - more counselling, more
accommodations for classwork, more chats with instructors, staff, coaches or RAs in the dorms.
And our adult learners have children, are often single parents, they may be caring for elders in their
family, juggling multiple low-wage jobs, and struggling to meet the costs of childcare, transportation, food and medical costs. Several of our adult learners did not succeed in college in the past and are taking a big risk coming back.
These are all very high-touch needs. Maine's community colleges must provide new and additional
resources to address these students' needs.
This money will allow us to hire more people to meet the needs of these students ---- including more tutors, more after-hours counseling, expanding the hours and staffing in existing language labs, libraries, more resident advisors, more partnerships with community support groups. It would also allow us to
provide deeper professional development to our current staff so they have the tools to identify and then
support our students who are struggling.
We are committed to not letting any of our students slip away because they couldn't get a call back, or
an appointment with a counselor, or academic tutoring. But we need this funding to do all that.
Thank you for your time and I am happy to entertain any questions now or for the work session.
185984:
Testimony from David Lewis, Jr.

~

Windham

In Support of L.D. 680 An Act to Support Higher Education in Maine by Providing Funds to Maine's

Community Colleges.

Joint Standing Committee on Education and CulturalAffairs March 17, 2025
Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Education
and Cultural Affairs, my name is David Lewis. I am a resident of Windham, ME and the Associate Dean of Academic Affairs at Central Maine Community College. I am here today in support of LD 680 which
would provide vital resources to institutions liI<e Central Maine Community College. Specifically, I want to
highlight the crucial role that tutoring services play in student achievement and the urgent need to expand these resources on community college campuses.
I've seen firsthand how impactful tutoring can be. As a student on the brink of academic dismissal in my
undergraduate degree, I struggled to balance multiple jobs, family responsibilities, and coursework. After
connecting with the tutoring center, I was able to turn things around, regain my academic standing, and ultimately graduate successfully. Now pursuing my doctoral degree, I am a living example of how tutoring has supported my academic success throughout my educational journey.
Tutoring services are essential for community college students, many of whom face unique challenges
that make their academic journey more difficult. Our students often juggle full-time jobs, family obligations, and financial constraints. Tutoring can be the critical difference between success and failure. Unfortunately, students who fail to utilize tutoring often earn grades that place them on academic
probation, suspension, or dismissal. When these students attempt to return from suspension or dismissal, we prioritize tutoring because we know it's key to their success.
At Central Maine Community College, tutoring services provide one-on-one support that helps students build confidence, understand complex material, and develop the skills they need to excel. Yet, despite its proven impact, our tutoring resources are stretched thin. Demand for tutoring continues to grow, yet we
are challenged with limited staffing, outdated resources, and a lack of dedicated space to provide adequate support.
Investing in tutoring services as part of the Student Success and Retention Bill would allow us to hire additional tutors, provide more flexible hours to meet the needs ofworking students, and improve our
facilities to create a more effective learning environment. By expanding tutoring resources, we can empower students to stay enrolled, complete their programs, and enter Maine's workforce prepared to
succeed.
Supporting this bill is an investment in Maine's future. It ensures that students at Central Maine
Community College --- and community colleges across the state -- have the resources they need to overcome obstacles, achieve their educational goals, and contribute to our economy. I urge you to prioritize this funding and support the success of our students.
Thank you foryour time and consideration.

Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Education
and Cultural Affairs, I am Dr. Elizabeth True from Sedgwick, and I serve as Vice President and Dean of
Students at Eastern Maine Community College. I am here today to testify in support of LD 680, An Act
to Support Higher Education in Maine by Providing Funds to Maine's Community Colleges. As Vice President, I oversee enrollment management and student success programs, designed to support the student from application through to graduation. Before I became Vice President, I was the satisfied
parent of a proud graduate of EMCC.

Students entering college for the first time encounter a variety of challenges, and learning how to identify and solve these diverse challenges is an ongoing process. Some students enter college with more
of the skills necessary for navigating the academic demands of independent learning and personal responsibility. These students maximize their learning opportunities in the small class sizes, practical training, and personal relationships with their instructors our college offers.

Other students enter with significant gaps in skills which can make their academic experience overwhelming and in some cases, unsuccessful. The transition from high school to college can be particularly challenging for those who expect that community college is basically 13"` grade. They may not know how to keep track of assignments and deadlines in courses without daily reminders. Studying and preparing for college classes is very different from completing high school homework.

At least 38% of our students are identified as first-generation college students, without the support and expertise of parents who are familiar with the challenges and resources of college. All of our traditional-
aged students survived a few years of pandemic schooling, and survival during lockdown was the
primary goal. They have now entered college without having experienced enough academic challenge
and support in high school, through no fault of their own, and are significantly behind in their academic, cognitive, and psychosocial development.

We also have an increasing number of students who received special education services in high school.
Our Accessibility Services office is ready to help them make the transition to college and access appropriate accommodations, but the process for accommodations in post-secondary settings is very different from K-12, and many students do not request accommodations in college for a variety of
reasons. EMCC is also experiencing increasing numbers of students who are on the autism spectrum. We also have a large population of adult learners who did not experience an educational system in their
youth that prioritized identifying and remediating learning problems.

Our staff are dedicated to our students' success, but their jobs have changed dramatically in the last five years. What used to be a five minute conversation with a student about how to complete a task is often
now at least a thirty minute session to compensate for their lack of executive functioning skills. We love
the opportunity to solve problems with students and help them achieve their goals, but I would have
much more confidence in our capacity to meet our current students' needs if we had additional staff who

.

could provide essential, individualized support as college navigators, supplemental instructors, and
learning specialists.
I very much appreciate the opportunity to discuss these needs with you today and hope you will
support LD 680 and by doing so, set more students up for success in learning the essential
trades and knowledge to be productive contributors to Maine's future.

RE: In support of L.D. 680 An Act to Support Higher Education in Maine by Providing Funds to Maine's Community Colleges
DATE: March, 17, 2025
Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and Members of the Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs, I am Jared Rubin, the Assistant Director of Residence Life at Central Maine Community College, and I am writing in strong support of L.D. 680, An Act to Support Higher Education in Maine by Providing Funds to Maine's Community Colleges.
Central Maine Community College has seen significant growth in its Residence Life program, expanding from 253 students in 2017, when I was a resident hall student, to 389 students today. This increase in student population is, in part, due to our initiative to rent out an entire hotel in Auburn to accommodate additional students. CMCC offers four distinct residence hall options, with three on-campus halls housing 253 students and one off-campus facility housing 136 students.
While this growth presents exciting opportunities, it has also introduced challenges for our Residence Life staff. In order to maintain a high level of support and engagement for our growing student body, I support L.D. 680 and the investment of $6 million in year one and $6.3 million in year two. This funding would enable us to address these challenges by hiring additional Resident Assistants (RAs) and Resident Directors (RDs), enhancing support services, and expanding student activities. These improvements are essential for ensuring a positive and supportive environment for all of our residents.
As an alumnus of Central Maine Community College, I've seen firsthand the importance of a supportive environment in our residence halls. From being a resident student to working as an RA, RD, and now Assistant Director of Residence Life, I understand how vital staff support is to student success. Adding more RAs and RDs would enhance the support system, ensuring students receive the assistance they need on their path to graduation.
I request your support of L.D. 680 and thank you for your time and consideration for supporting CMCC's students moving forward.

Lewiston, Maine Administrator at Central Maine Community College, Auburn, Maine

Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and Members of the Joint Standing Committee on Education and
Cultural Affairs, I am Jean Blais, Student Services Administrator at Central Maine Community College, and I am writing in strong support of LD 680, An Act to Support Higher Education in Maine by Providing
Funds to Maine's Community Colleges.
Maine Community Colleges serve a diverse student population, including first-generation students,
working adults, parents, and individuals facing financial and personal challenges. Many of these students
struggle with stress, anxiety, depression, and other mental health conditions that significantly impact their academic success and overall well-being.
As an administrator at Central Maine Community College, I witness these mental health challenges
firsthand. Students struggling with mental health issues often face difficulties concentrating, completing
assignments, and engaging in class. Without proper support, many underperform academically, withdraw
from courses, or ultimately drop out of college.
Currently, Central Maine Community College has only one mental health counselor available on campus just one day a week for in-person counseling, with online counseling offered on other days. While virtual options provide some level of support, they do not fully replace the need for in-person services, particularly for students in crisis. Due to the high demand for mental health services, counselors' schedules are full, leading to long wait times for students seeking help. Many students who need immediate support are left
without timely access to the care they require, exacerbating their struggles and increasing the likelihood of them leaving college.
This issue extends beyond student well-being--it directly impacts student retention, academic achievement, and the future of Maine's workforce. Providing the necessary supports for student success is crucial to ensuring students have the resources to thrive.
I strongly urge funding for LD 680, the Student Retention and Success Bill. This bill would provide much-
needed resources to expand mental health services, including hiring additional counselors to reduce wait
times and ensure students receive timely, in-person support. Increased access to counseling can make the
difference between a student persisting through their education or dropping out due to unaddressed mental
health struggles.
I respectfully request your support for LD 680. Investing in our students is an investment in Maine's
future----ensuring that students receive the support they need to thrive academically, graduate successfully, and contribute to our workforce and communities.
Thank you for your time and consideration.

Of the 1,026 community colleges throughout the country, I am proud to represent one of Maine's
seven community colleges. According to the American Association of Community Colleges,
approximately 40% of all undergraduate students in the United States are currently studying at a
community college. While impressive to know that two out of every five college students are
enrolled in a community college, you may be further surprised to learn that roughly 60% of all
bachelor's degree holders in the United States have earned college credits from a community college at some point throughout their educational journey. Our students, though resilient, often
carry substantial burdens.

Unlike our four-year university partners, community college students primarily attend school part-time. This is for a variety of reasons, but many of which revolve around the reality that our
students are significant financial providers and often the primary, or only, caregivers for their
family. 60% of part-tirne students work full-time jobs, and over 40% of full-tirne students work full-time jobs while enrolled at community colleges. The numbers are similar at SMCC. There is
a direct correlation to the number of credits a student eams each semester and their time to graduation. Graduation, retention, and student success rates among community college students lag behind their four-year university counterparts; this, however, has little to do with one's
intellectual capacity in the classroom. Research leaders in higher education point to something else: LIFE, in all capital letters, presents external barriers which far-too-ofien prevent community college students from earning obtaining their educational goals in a timely manner, or at all.
We know that students succeed at a higher rate when they have appropriate supports and strong
networks that can pick them up or keep them on track. For students who are the first to attend
college in their family, which account for one-third of our students, it is an even more imposing
task when your family does know how to support you because college is something of an enigma. For students with disabilities, who account for nearly one quarter of community college
students, college-provided support is equally invaluable. These are but two of myriad reasons
why your support is so vital.
Historically, community colleges have been underfunded and under resourced, yet they are
responsible for serving some of our most vulnerable neighbors. Still, we persevere and continue
to be an engine that lifts communities and propels local and state economies. At the community
colleges, we will continue to do all we can to remove barriers to students' success. With your increased support, we can provide the support our students deserve, and we can attract and retain
the innovative teachers, advisors, and workforce development that our communities need. I have

Testimony in Support of
LD 680, An Act to Support Higher Education in Maine by Providing Funds to Maine's
Community Colleges Presented to the Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs
March 17, 2025
Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and Esteemed Members of the Joint Standing Committee
on Education and Cultural Affairs, my name is Mattie Daughtry. I serve as President of the Maine
Senate and proudly represent Senate District 23, including Brunswick, Freeport, Haipswell, Pownal,
Chebeague Island, and part of Yarmouth. Today, I am honored to present LD 680, "An Act to
Support Higher Education in Maine by Providing Funds to Maine's Community Colleges."
Maine's community colleges are one of the most effective tools we have to expand educational
opportunity, strengthen our workforce, and help Mainers build successful careers. Our seven
community colleges serve a diverse group of students----many of whom are balancing school with
jobs, family obligations and other responsibilities. They are future nurses, teachers, mechanics, IT professionals and small business owners. Their success is Maine's success.
We know that pursuing a degree or credential of value is not always easy, particularly for students
who are also caretakers, first-generation college students or those returning to school after time in the workforce. Community colleges have noted that these students need additional support to help them
stay enrolled, complete their education, and transition into Maine's workforce. That is why LD 680
provides essential ongoing funding to ensure our community colleges have the resources they need to
continue offering high-quality support services to students across the state.
In recent years, Maine's community colleges have seen historic enrollment increases, largely due to targeted investments like the Free Community College initiative and workforce training programs.
However, we know that increased enrollment also brings increased need. More students require
support to complete their education and earn a credential of value. Furthermore, MCCS has
emphasized, and I agree, that these supports are essential for helping students--particularly firstgeneration and low-income learners---overcome barriers to completing their education.
LD 680 provides critical funding to ensure that Maine's community colleges can continue meeting
the needs of our current students, who are our future workforce.
A state appropriation of $6 million in FY2026 and $6.3 million in FY2027 would expand student
persistence and completion support by:
Expanding academic counseling and advising services to help students plan their educational pathways, saving them time and money and ensuring they stay on track. Increasing access to tutoring services and extending the hours of writing and math labs to provide academic support where it is most needed.

responsibilities.
Providing emergency aid to assist students facing unexpected financial crises that might otherwise force them to drop out.
Strengthening and supporting Transfer ME, ensuring students have clear and supported pathways
to continue their education in the University of Maine System or at a different Maine institution via
the NEBHE Transfer Guarantee. We have already seen the transformative impact of investments in our community college system.
Since its launch, the Free College program has enrolled 12,625 students----surpassing the original goal of 8,000 by 158%.
The number of students who transfer from MCCS to the University of Maine System has increased
by 50%. Programs that help students persist and succeed are critical not only for student success but also for
meeting Maine's workforce needs. At a time when employers are struggling to find trained workers
in key industries, our community colleges are an essential part of the solution.
By passing LD 680, we are making a smart investment in Maine's future. These funds will strengthen
the foundation of our workforce, provide economic opportunity for thousands of Mainers and support the continued success of our community colleges. I respectfully urge the Committee's support for this bill, and I would be happy to answer any
questions.

Testimony from Tobby Bragdon
Gray
In Support of L.D. 680 An Act to Support Higher Education in Maine by Providing Funds to Maine's Community Colleges.
Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs
March 17, 2025
Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and Members of the Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs, I am Tobby Bragdon, Academic Dean at Central Maine Community College, and I am writing in strong support of LD 680, An Act to Support Higher Education in Maine by Providing Funds to Maine's Community Colleges. I appreciate your leadership and commitment to ensuring that Maine's community college students have access to the critical resources they need to succeed.
At Central Maine Community College, we have seen how expanded tutoring programs, targeted supplemental instruction, and other academic supports can dramatically improve student outcomes. By providing an additional $6 million in the first year and $6.3 million in the second year, LD 680 would allow us to extend the reach of these services and help students overcome barriers to success. Increased academic supports not only boost retention and completion rates but also create a path toward meaningful careers and financial stability.
I was once a student at Kennebec Valley Community College. That personal experience--and the guidance, tutoring, and supplemental instruction I received--shaped my understanding of how deeply these services matter. Now, as Academic Dean at Central Maine Community College, I can attest that such support is often the difference between a student thriving in their program or feeling overwhelmed and giving up on their educational goals.
I respectfully request your support of LD 680. Thank you for your time and consideration, and for your continued commitment to opening doors for Maine's community college students.
